Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| sort - severity
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Dysphoria IoT Botnet Adds Blockchain C2 and Victim Relays After JackSkid Disruption

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Dysphoria, an Internet of Things (IoT) botnet line tracked by CNCERT and XLab, has adopted blockchain-based name services and infected-device relays after a March law-enforcement operation against JackSkid infrastructure. The researchers say the design makes the botnet harder to disrupt. CNCERT, China's national computer emergency response team, and XLab, the threat-intelligence lab of Chinese

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] IoT weak-credential entry — SSH/Telnet failed-auth burst then success · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dysphoria botnet C2 server-list fetch — HTTP GET :9000/nodes?key=meowmeowmeow · [LLM] Dysphoria blockchain C2 resolution — ENS (.eth) / SNS (.sol) name lookups · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Dysphoria botnet C2 server-list fetch — HTTP GET :9000/nodes?key=meowmeowmeow AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Dysphoria/JackSkid DDoS sample retrieving its dynamic relay list from a distribution node via the fixed request `http://<node>:9000/nodes?key=meowmeowmeow`, and direct connections to XLab-confirmed C2/relay IPs. This is the botnet's uniquely-fingerprinted C2 rendezvous, not generic beaconing. Rationale: The URI `/nodes?key=meowmeowmeow` on TCP/9000 is the exact distribution-node request string documented in the XLab primary report — a fixed path + hardcoded key = near-zero FP. IPs are the XLab-confirmed C2/relay set; I dropped the article's 194.87.198.x / 194.58.38.x IPs because the primary XLab source does not list them (uncorroborated). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/dysphoria/ • https://securityaffairs.com/189710/cyber-crime/global-law-enforcement-operation-targets-aisuru-kimwolf-jackskid-botnet-operators.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal dev/monitoring service listening on port 9000 (SonarQube, Prometheus pushgateway, PHP-FPM) contacted by health checks — but never with the /nodes?key=meowmeowmeow URI
  • Custom internal API that happens to expose a /nodes endpoint (would lack the meowmeowmeow key)
  • Security scanner replaying the IOC URI during a purple-team exercise
  • NAT/proxy egress collapsing many hosts to one SourceIP, inflating hit counts
Suppression filter
// The meowmeowmeow key makes the URI branch self-filtering; scope the IP branch to port 9000 only
| where (RemoteUrl has "meowmeowmeow") or (RemotePort == 9000 and RemoteIP in ("217.60.195.160","76.164.203.171","92.42.100.131","78.153.155.152","144.31.38.215"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the matching host is the client (SourceIP) not the server; verify the full URI contains `key=meowmeowmeow` and the destination port is 9000. Pull the initiating process on the endpoint if EDR-covered. 2) Contain: block egress to the five C2/relay IPs and to :9000 for the host at the firewall; isolate the device; if it is IoT, power-cycle and reset credentials/firmware. 3) Hunt: pivot on the destination IPs across all netflow for other internal bots/relays, and run the ENS/SNS DNS hunt (companion UC) to find how the host obtained the node list.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has "/nodes" and RemoteUrl has "meowmeowmeow")
    or (RemotePort == 9000 and RemoteIP in ("217.60.195.160","76.164.203.171","92.42.100.131","78.153.155.152","144.31.38.215"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (RequestURL has "/nodes" and RequestURL has "meowmeowmeow")
    or (DestinationPort == 9000 and DestinationIP in ("217.60.195.160","76.164.203.171","92.42.100.131","78.153.155.152","144.31.38.215"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Dysphoria Botnet C2 Server-List Fetch
id: 8f2b1c44-9d3e-4a17-b0c2-3e7a1f9d6c22
description: Detects the Dysphoria/JackSkid DDoS sample fetching its relay node list from a distribution node using the fixed /nodes?key=meowmeowmeow URI on port 9000.
references:

  condition: selection
level: high

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=9000
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^(217\.60\.195\.160|76\.164\.203\.171|92\.42\.100\.131|78\.153\.155\.152|144\.31\.38\.215)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="/nodes" Web.uri_query="key=meowmeowmeow") OR (Web.dest_port=9000 AND Web.dest IN ("217.60.195.160","76.164.203.171","92.42.100.131","78.153.155.152","144.31.38.215")) by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="/nodes" Web.uri_query="key=meowmeowmeow") OR (Web.dest_port=9000 AND Web.dest IN ("217.60.195.160","76.164.203.171","92.42.100.131","78.153.155.152","144.31.38.215")) by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Dysphoria blockchain C2 resolution — ENS (.eth) / SNS (.sol) name lookups AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoints resolving Dysphoria's blockchain-based C2 records (m3rnbvs5d.eth, burrberry.eth, ukranianhorseriding.eth, 24carnforth2merseyside.sol) and, more broadly, any `.eth`/`.sol` pseudo-TLD lookup — a resolution model highly anomalous in enterprise DNS and central to how Dysphoria hides its controllers. Rationale: The four ENS/SNS domains are confirmed in the XLab primary report (ukranianhorseriding.eth added from that source, which the THN article omitted). The `.eth`/`.sol` TLD branch is a broader hunt: these pseudo-TLDs are not part of standard DNS and are anomalous in nearly every enterprise, making even the wide match tractable. Datadog left empty — the provided windows.sysmon field set has no DNS-query attribute. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/dysphoria/ • https://www.gm7.org/archives/133344
ATT&CKT1568 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or crypto/web3 user resolving a legitimate ENS/SNS name via a browser wallet extension (MetaMask, Phantom)
  • Browser prefetch/typo of a `.eth`/`.sol` string in a URL bar
  • Threat-intel or blockchain research tooling querying ENS resolvers
  • DNS-over-HTTPS gateways that proxy ENS (eth.link) — the named-domain branch stays high-fidelity even if the TLD branch is noisy
Suppression filter
// Keep named domains alert-grade; gate the broad TLD branch to non-browser initiators
| where Name in~ ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","ukranianhorseriding.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol") or (Name endswith ".eth" or Name endswith ".sol")
Response runbook
1) Triage: separate hits on the four named C2 domains (alert-grade, act immediately) from generic .eth/.sol hits (review the querying process/user for legitimate wallet use). 2) Contain: for named-domain hits, isolate the device and sinkhole/block the ENS gateway egress; capture the resolved IP and cross-block it. 3) Hunt: pivot the same source host to the :9000/nodes?key=meowmeowmeow fetch (companion UC) and to outbound connections to the XLab C2 IP set to confirm active bot/relay behavior.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".eth" or RemoteUrl endswith ".sol"
    or RemoteUrl in~ ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","ukranianhorseriding.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith ".eth" or Name endswith ".sol"
    or Name in~ ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","ukranianhorseriding.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Dysphoria Blockchain C2 ENS/SNS Domain Resolution
id: c1a7d9e2-4b83-4f56-9a1e-72d4c0b8f331
description: Detects DNS resolution of Dysphoria botnet ENS/SNS C2 domains and of .eth/.sol pseudo-TLDs used for blockchain-based command-and-control.
references:
  - https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/dysphoria/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/dysphoria-iot-botnet-adds-blockchain-c2.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1568
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection_named:
    query:
      - 'm3rnbvs5d.eth'
      - 'burrberry.eth'
      - 'ukranianhorseriding.eth'
      - '24carnforth2merseyside.sol'
  selection_tld:
    query|endswith:
      - '.eth'
      - '.sol'
  condition: selection_named or selection_tld
level: high
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(m3rnbvs5d\.eth|burrberry\.eth|ukranianhorseriding\.eth|24carnforth2merseyside\.sol|\.eth$|\.sol$)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","ukranianhorseriding.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol") OR DNS.query="*.eth" OR DNS.query="*.sol") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.record_type | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","ukranianhorseriding.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol") OR DNS.query="*.eth" OR DNS.query="*.sol") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.record_type | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
IoT weak-credential entry — SSH/Telnet failed-auth burst then success AIExploitation Medium
Detects the Dysphoria primary propagation vector: Telnet/SSH weak-password guessing against internet-facing Linux/IoT hosts, surfaced as a burst of failed logons (optionally followed by an accepted login) from a single source. Targets the article's stated 'most consistent way in'. Rationale: The article and both CNCERT/XLab lists agree weak Telnet/SSH credentials are Dysphoria's most consistent infection vector; the detection keys on sshd/telnetd failed-auth bursts on internet-facing hosts (T1110.001/T1078.001). Threshold-based, so no Sigma; Falcon/CloudWatch empty because IoT/Linux SSH endpoints are typically outside FDR/AWS coverage here. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/dysphoria/ • https://www.gm7.org/archives/133344
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1078.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured backup/monitoring agent hammering sshd with a stale credential
  • CI/CD or Ansible runner with an expired key generating repeated auth failures
  • Legitimate internet-wide scanner (Shodan/Censys) probing an exposed device
  • Locked-out admin retrying a forgotten password
  • Password rotation not yet propagated to a service account
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !startswith "10." and SrcIP !startswith "192.168." and not (ipv4_is_in_range(SrcIP, "172.16.0.0/12"))    // exclude internal automation ranges; keep external guessing
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the source IP is internal/known-automation or external; confirm whether any 'Accepted password/publickey' followed the burst on the same host+user (successful guess). 2) Contain: if a success followed, isolate the device, kill active SSH sessions, rotate/replace the credential, and block the source IP; disable Telnet and internet-facing remote management. 3) Hunt: from any compromised host, pivot to outbound :9000/nodes?key=meowmeowmeow fetches and ENS/SNS lookups (companion UCs) to confirm botnet enrolment, and sweep other internet-facing devices for the same source IP.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| where Protocol =~ "Ssh" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sshd","telnetd")
| summarize Failures = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Users = dcount(AccountName)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where Failures >= 20    // 20 failed SSH/Telnet auths in 10m from one source = guessing burst
| order by Failures desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName in ("sshd","telnetd")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Failed password","authentication failure","Invalid user","Failed login")
| extend SrcIP = extract(@"from ([0-9]{1,3}(?:\.[0-9]{1,3}){3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(SrcIP)
| summarize Failures = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by Computer, SrcIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Failures >= 20    // empirical guessing-burst threshold
| order by Failures desc
source:linux.syslog (@process.name:sshd OR @process.name:telnetd) ("Failed password" OR "authentication failure" OR "Invalid user")
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as failures from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="failure" Authentication.app IN ("sshd","ssh","telnetd","telnet") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user _time span=10m | where failures >= 20 | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count as failures from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="failure" Authentication.app IN ("sshd","ssh","telnetd","telnet") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user _time span=10m | where failures >= 20 | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - failures
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("194.87.198.208", "194.87.198.104", "194.58.38.79", "194.58.38.49", "194.58.38.96") or RemoteUrl has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth", "burrberry.eth", "24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["194.87.198.208", "194.87.198.104", "194.58.38.79", "194.58.38.49", "194.58.38.96"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["m3rnbvs5d.eth", "burrberry.eth", "24carnforth2merseyside.sol"]);
ImNetworkSession

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Anubis ransomware execution via distinctive /WIPEMODE /PFAD= /KEY= command-line flags
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anubis ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via hardcoded /for=norealvolume artifact · [LLM] Anubis ransomware mass file encryption — .anubis extension write burst · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anubis ransomware execution via distinctive /WIPEMODE /PFAD= /KEY= command-line flags AIInstallation High
Hunts the Anubis ransomware payload (family that hit Coca-Cola's Fairlife subsidiary) by its unique command-line switch set. Anubis requires operator-supplied flags — /KEY= to start encryption, /elevated to self-escalate, /PFAD= to exclude paths, /PATH= to target a directory, and /WIPEMODE to irreversibly zero files instead of encrypting. The /WIPEMODE and German-language /PFAD= tokens are near-unique to this family. Rationale: Uses the Anubis-specific CLI switches /WIPEMODE, /PFAD= (German 'Pfad'=path), /KEY= and /elevated documented by Trend Micro; /WIPEMODE and /PFAD= are effectively unique to this family, making this very high fidelity even absent hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/anubis-ransomware-adds-wiper-to-destroy-files-beyond-recovery/ • https://blog.barracuda.com/2025/07/11/wipe--leak--extort--the-crazy-hybrid-playbook-of-anubis-ransomwa
ATT&CKT1486 T1485 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup or archival tool that happens to use a /KEY= licensing argument together with an /elevated relaunch flag
  • Custom internal admin scripts that pass a /PATH= directory argument (mitigated — this rule requires /PFAD= or /WIPEMODE specifically)
  • Security-team detonation of Anubis samples in a sandbox/lab host
  • Red-team or purple-team ransomware simulation using the real Anubis binary
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","backup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/WIPEMODE" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/PFAD=")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent process; confirm the binary is unsigned/newly-dropped and check the SHA256 against Trend Micro Anubis IOCs. Note whether /WIPEMODE is present — if so recovery is impossible, treat as destructive. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host immediately via EDR, kill the process tree, and block the binary hash org-wide; alert IR lead given active encryption/wiping. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256/parent across all hosts, look for the paired vssadmin norealvolume shadow-copy deletion and mass .anubis file renames on this and neighbouring hosts, and review recent RDP/WinRM logons to the host for the ingress account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/WIPEMODE","/PFAD=")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "/KEY=" and ProcessCommandLine has "/elevated")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has_any ("/WIPEMODE","/PFAD=")
   or (CommandLine has "/KEY=" and CommandLine has "/elevated")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via hardcoded /for=norealvolume artifact AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Anubis's pre-encryption inhibit-recovery step. The payload shells out 'vssadmin delete shadows /for=norealvolume /all /quiet' — the literal placeholder volume 'norealvolume' is a hardcoded Anubis artifact that distinguishes it from routine vssadmin shadow maintenance. Rationale: The full string 'vssadmin delete shadows /for=norealvolume /all /quiet' is documented by Trend Micro as Anubis's exact shadow-copy deletion command; the bogus 'norealvolume' volume name is a hardcoded artifact absent from any legitimate admin usage, giving near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.securityweek.com/anubis-ransomware-packs-a-wiper-to-permanently-delete-files/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None realistic for the 'norealvolume' token — it is not a real volume so no legitimate admin or backup product supplies it
  • A malware analyst re-running the Anubis binary in a lab
  • Purple-team ransomware emulation deliberately reproducing the Anubis vssadmin string
  • A YARA/AV signature test harness echoing the command into a log without executing it
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a high-confidence hit — confirm the parent process (the ransomware payload) and its SHA256, and check whether encryption/.anubis renames have already begun on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host via EDR now, kill the parent process tree, and disable the executing account; shadow copies are already gone so prioritise stopping spread over local recovery. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same parent hash, the /WIPEMODE|/PFAD= command lines, and .anubis file writes; check backup infrastructure and hypervisors (ESXi/Nutanix) for the same actor given Anubis's cross-platform VM targeting.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows" and ProcessCommandLine has "norealvolume"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe"
| where CommandLine has "delete shadows" and CommandLine has "norealvolume"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis ransomware mass file encryption — .anubis extension write burst AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact stage where Anubis appends the .anubis extension to encrypted files (or zeroes them in wiper mode). Aggregates file writes/renames to .anubis per host and process so a single encrypting binary touching many files fires once, not per file. Rationale: Anubis appends the .anubis extension to encrypted files (Trend Micro); a burst of >50 distinct .anubis writes from one process on one host is textbook mass-encryption impact and cleanly distinguishes ransomware from any legitimate single-file usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/anubis-ransomware-group-overview-and-evolution
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher extracting an Anubis sample set where files are already named *.anubis (mitigated by the >50-distinct-path threshold plus single-process grouping)
  • Backup/AV quarantine that copies encrypted victim files preserving the .anubis name (would show a backup-agent parent, not the ransomware binary)
  • Threat-intel repo sync that writes many .anubis IOC sample files to a security team share
  • DFIR evidence collection copying an encrypted volume onto an analysis host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","msmpeng.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName is an unsigned recently-dropped binary (not a backup or AV agent) and check FileCount trajectory — active climbing count means encryption in progress. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, kill the writing process, block its hash, and snapshot/protect any remaining unencrypted shares and hypervisor datastores. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating SHA256 across the fleet, correlate with the vssadmin norealvolume and /WIPEMODE command-line detections, and check ESXi/Nutanix and NAS telemetry since Anubis encrypts those platforms too.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".anubis"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where FileCount > 50
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".anubis"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50
| order by FileCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.anubis OR *.ANUBIS OR *.Anubis)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.anubis$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=fileCount))
| fileCount > 50
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.anubis" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where distinct_paths > 50
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.anubis" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where distinct_paths > 50
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anomalous first-seen sign-in with valid EY account to GitHub/Azure/Jira (ShinyHunters supply-chain creds) AIDelivery Low
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins to the three cloud/SaaS platforms named in the EY breach (GitHub, Azure, Jira/Atlassian) from an ASN or country never before seen for that user in a 30-day baseline. Targets the ShinyHunters technique of authenticating with valid credentials stolen from a compromised upstream supplier rather than exploiting EY directly. Rationale: Anchored on the three environments the article explicitly names as breached (Jira, GitHub, Azure) plus the stated supply-chain valid-account vector; the new-ASN/new-country anti-join against a 30d baseline turns 'valid login' into 'valid login from infrastructure this user has never used', which is the only way to catch stolen-credential reuse absent any IOC. Cross-checked ShinyHunters TTPs (T1078.004/T1199) against EclecticIQ, Microsoft, and Huntress writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/shinyhunters-calling-financially-motivated-data-extortion-group-targeting-enterprise-cloud-applications • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/13/defending-saas-based-applications-against-shinyhunters-oauth-abuse/ • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1199 T1195.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee traveling or on a new mobile carrier/VPN egress producing a first-seen ASN or country
  • New hire's first-ever sign-in to GitHub/Azure/Jira (no baseline exists yet)
  • MSP/consultant legitimately accessing tenant resources from their own corporate ASN
  • Corporate egress IP re-homed to a new ISP/ASN after a network change
  • Cloud-to-cloud service traffic where the user's token is replayed from a datacenter ASN
Suppression filter
| where ClientAppUsed != "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" or UserAgent has_any ("python","curl","Go-http","axios","node-fetch")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the flagged sign-in's IPAddress/ASN/UserAgent and compare to the user's 30-day norm; confirm whether the ASN belongs to a hosting/VPS provider (ShinyHunters commonly egresses from cloud infra) vs a residential/corporate ISP. Check for MFA satisfaction method and any concurrent new MFA-device registration in AuditLogs. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and temporarily block the source IP/ASN via Conditional Access. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every resource that account touched across SigninLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs in the window, look for the same ASN authenticating as other users, and check GitHub/Jira audit logs for bulk repo/ticket reads.

let recent = 1d;
let SensitiveApps = dynamic(["GitHub","Azure","Windows Azure Service Management","Jira","Atlassian"]);
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta

| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize by AccountUpn, Country;

| where ErrorCode == 0

| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent

SigninLogs

| where ResultType == 0

| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName, AutonomousSystemNumber
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, tostring(Location), AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Single identity authenticating to Jira + GitHub + Azure within one hour (ShinyHunters cross-SaaS credential reuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts one Entra ID identity successfully signing in to two or more of the exact platforms the article says were breached with the same stolen credentials — Jira/Atlassian, GitHub, and Azure — inside a one-hour window. Flags the ShinyHunters pattern of rapidly pivoting a single valid credential set across multiple SaaS/cloud tenants. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's central claim — the same stolen EY credential set breached 'Jira, GitHub, and Azure environments' — as a per-identity fan-out across those exact platform names within a tight window, which is far more specific than a generic impossible-travel rule. ShinyHunters' documented cross-tenant valid-account pivoting (EclecticIQ, Microsoft, Huntress) corroborates the shape. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/shinyhunters-calling-financially-motivated-data-extortion-group-targeting-enterprise-cloud-applications • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/13/defending-saas-based-applications-against-shinyhunters-oauth-abuse/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/defending-against-shinyhunters-tactics-and-breaches

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps/platform engineers who legitimately use GitHub, Azure DevOps and Jira together every hour of the workday
  • CI/CD service or automation accounts federating into all three platforms via SSO
  • A developer's SSO session refreshing tokens for multiple linked apps in one burst
  • Sprint-planning workflows where an engineer opens Jira, a linked GitHub PR, and Azure Portal in sequence
  • Break-glass admin performing a legitimate cross-platform incident review
Suppression filter
| where array_length(SourceIPs) > 1 or array_length(Countries) > 1
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the account is an engineer/DevOps role that normally spans all three platforms (check IdentityInfo Department/JobTitle) — if so, verify all sign-ins share the user's usual IP/ASN. Escalate if the platforms were reached from >1 distinct ASN or a hosting-provider IP. 2) CONTAIN: For an unexplained hit, revoke sessions, reset credentials, and disable any OAuth app consents or new MFA methods added by the account in the window. 3) HUNT: Query GitHub audit log for repo clones/downloads, Jira for bulk issue exports/searches, and Azure activity for resource enumeration by the same principal; pivot on shared source IP to find other affected identities.

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

SecurityEvent

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

Critical

Public Exploit Released for Patched vBulletin Pre-Auth Code Execution Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 8 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Public exploit details released on July 27 show how an unauthenticated request can reach PHP's eval() function inside vBulletin and execute code on an unpatched forum server. The attack requires no account, administrative access, or interaction from another user. SSD Secure Disclosure lists vBulletin 6.2.1 and earlier, and 6.1.6 and earlier, as affected, but does not give a lower version

Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Unpatched vBulletin instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-61511 (below 6.2.2 / 6.1.6) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via ajax/render/pagenav operator-heavy pagenav[pagenumber] · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Web service account (php-fpm/httpd/nginx/w3wp) spawning shell after vBulletin RCE
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via ajax/render/pagenav operator-heavy pagenav[pagenumber] AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound web requests to the public vBulletin route ajax/render/pagenav where the pagenav[pagenumber] value carries PHP operators (notably the XOR '^', parentheses, arithmetic) instead of a plain integer — the 'phpfuck' letter-free payload SSD's PoC feeds to runMaths()->eval(). A legitimate page number is digits only, so any operator/paren in that parameter is high-fidelity for CVE-2026-61511 exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact article strings ajax/render/pagenav and pagenav[pagenumber], plus the corroborated XOR '^' bypass character that makes runMaths() reach eval(); a page number is normally digits-only so any operator/paren is near-zero-FP. Second sources confirm the route and the '^' filter gap. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/critical-vbulletin-vulnerability/ • https://securityonline.info/critical-pre-auth-rce-vbulletin-flaw-allows-full-server-compromise-poc-available/ • https://www.acunetix.com/vulnerabilities/web/vbulletin-pre-auth-rce-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest/red-team replaying the SSD PoC against the forum
  • Automated web vulnerability scanners (Acunetix/Nuclei) firing CVE-2026-61511 templates
  • Legitimate but unusual pagination plugins that URL-encode brackets (rare — still won't contain '^' or parens)
  • Security researchers validating patch status internally
Suppression filter
| where not (csUserAgent has_any ("Nuclei","Acunetix","Nessus","nikto") and cIP in ("10.","172.16.","192.168."))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (uri_query/body) and confirm pagenav[pagenumber] contains operators/XOR; check scStatus — a 200 with an unexpected body length suggests command output was returned. Note src IP and user-agent. 2) Contain: block the src IP at the WAF/edge, and if the response indicates code executed, isolate the web host and rotate any secrets readable by the web service account. 3) Hunt: confirm the server's vBulletin build (<6.2.2 for 6.2.x, <6.1.6 for 6.1.x) is unpatched; pivot to UC 'Web service account spawning shell' on the same host around the request time.

| where csUriQuery has "pagenav"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web service account (php-fpm/httpd/nginx/w3wp) spawning shell after vBulletin RCE AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-61511: the vBulletin PHP worker or web server process (php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd, nginx, apache2, w3wp.exe) spawning an interactive shell or download utility. SSD's PoC rebuilds PHP's system() to run an OS command, so a shell/curl/wget child of the web tier is the on-host tell. Rationale: Article states the PoC rebuilds PHP's system() and returns OS command output over HTTP, so the highest-fidelity host signal is the web-tier account (php-fpm/httpd/nginx/w3wp) parenting a shell or curl/wget. Parent+child pairing keeps FPs down; machine accounts excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/critical-vbulletin-vulnerability/ • https://securityonline.info/critical-pre-auth-rce-vbulletin-flaw-allows-full-server-compromise-poc-available/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP app legitimately shelling to ImageMagick/ffmpeg/backup scripts
  • Cron or deployment jobs running under the web service account
  • Admin debugging the forum via a web-triggered maintenance script
  • Monitoring agents invoking curl/wget from the web user context
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe","wget","wget.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","localhost","http://169.254"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — reconnaissance (whoami/id), download (curl/wget to external IP), or reverse-shell strings confirm compromise; correlate the parent PID with the web request time from UC1. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and rotate credentials/keys accessible to the web service account. 3) Hunt: search for dropped webshells/files written by the web account, new cron/systemd persistence, and outbound connections from php-fpm/w3wp to unfamiliar IPs.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php","httpd","httpd.exe","apache2","nginx","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","whoami","whoami.exe","curl","curl.exe","wget","wget.exe","certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessTokenElevation, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Unpatched vBulletin instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-61511 (below 6.2.2 / 6.1.6) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces managed hosts carrying a vBulletin build affected by CVE-2026-61511 so the exposed self-hosted, internet-facing population can be prioritized for the 6.2.2 upgrade. The article states the live risk concentrates in self-hosted forums that never applied the late-June fix. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-61511) and the article's fixed/affected build boundaries (fixed 6.2.2; affected 6.2.1 and earlier, 6.1.6 and earlier) to prioritize patching; keyed on TVM's CVE mapping so it executes as-is. IsInternetFacing join focuses on the exposed population the article flags. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acunetix.com/vulnerabilities/web/vbulletin-pre-auth-rce-vulnerability/ • https://cyberpress.org/critical-vbulletin-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud-hosted vBulletin already patched by the vendor but not yet re-scanned by TVM
  • Internal/test forum instances not internet-exposed (lower priority, not false)
  • Version string reported by TVM lagging an applied hotfix
  • Non-production staging copies flagged alongside production
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely below 6.2.2 (6.2.x) or 6.1.6 (6.1.x) and whether the host is internet-facing. 2) Contain: schedule the emergency 6.2.2 upgrade / branch patch for exposed instances; apply WAF virtual-patch blocking operator-heavy pagenav[pagenumber] in the interim (see UC1). 3) Hunt: retro-search web logs (UC1) and web-tier process spawns (UC2) on each vulnerable host back to the late-June patch date to rule out exploitation during the ~4-week exposure window.

| order by IsInternetFacing desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
