Process Ghosting: executable created then deleted while backing a live process AIInstallation Medium
Behavioral hunt for Cruciferra's Process Ghosting variant — a temporary image file is created and unlinked from disk around process launch so EDR memory scanners have nothing to scan. Correlates a FileCreated + FileDeleted of the same .exe/.dll in a user-writable staging path by the same process within a tight window. Rationale: Process Ghosting is the article's headline technique (create-then-delete the image backing a running process). Same-PID create+delete of an .exe/.dll in a staging path within 2 minutes is a workable behavioral proxy since Defender/Sysmon do not directly surface the NtSetInformationFile(DELETE) primitive. Hunting tier due to installer/self-update noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/unpacking-cruciferra-analysis-sophisticated-crypter-service • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/cruciferra-crypter-process-ghosting/
ATT&CKT1036.004 T1055.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Software installers extracting a temp EXE/DLL then cleaning it up (Squirrel, NSIS, MSI custom actions)
  • Application self-update routines staging and deleting update payloads in AppData
  • Browser/Electron apps writing and removing temporary module caches
  • Antivirus scanning that copies then deletes a temp scan artifact
  • Build/CI agents on developer hosts creating and removing temp binaries
Suppression filter
| where CreatorProc !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","update.exe","squirrel.exe","7z.exe","7zg.exe") and not (FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\" and CreatorProc has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","teams.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort by shortest LifeSec — a sub-5-second create/delete of an EXE by a Mono/dotnet or side-loaded parent, especially followed by a suspended child process, is high-signal; installers usually run tens of seconds. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture a memory image before reboot (the ghosted payload only lives in RAM), suspend/kill the associated process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate the creating process to the BYOVD driver load, 'putty' Run key, and C2 IOCs; carve the deleted file from the memory image for hashing.
let Window = 2m;
let Created = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
    | where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
    | where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll"
    | project DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, CreateTime=Timestamp, CreatorProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, CreatorPid=InitiatingProcessId, SHA256;
let Deleted = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
    | where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll"
    | project DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, DeleteTime=Timestamp, DeleterPid=InitiatingProcessId;
Created
| join kind=inner Deleted on DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath
| where DeleteTime between (CreateTime .. CreateTime + Window)
| where CreatorPid == DeleterPid
| project CreateTime, DeleteTime, LifeSec=datetime_diff('second', DeleteTime, CreateTime), DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, CreatorProc, SHA256
| order by CreateTime desc
let Window = 2m;
let Created = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EventType == "FileCreated"
    | where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
    | where TargetFileName endswith ".exe" or TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
    | project DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, CreateTime=TimeGenerated, CreatorProc=ActingProcessName, CreatorPid=ActingProcessId;
let Deleted = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EventType == "FileDeleted"
    | where TargetFileName endswith ".exe" or TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
    | project DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, DeleteTime=TimeGenerated, DeleterPid=ActingProcessId;
Created
| join kind=inner Deleted on DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| where DeleteTime between (CreateTime .. CreateTime + Window)
| where CreatorPid == DeleterPid
| project CreateTime, DeleteTime, LifeSec=datetime_diff('second', DeleteTime, CreateTime), DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, CreatorProc
| order by CreateTime desc
#event_simpleName=/^File(Written|Deleted)$/ (TargetFileName=/\\(AppData\\Local\\Temp|ProgramData|Users\\Public)\\/i TargetFileName=/\.(exe|dll)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId, TargetFileName], function=collect([event_simpleName]))
| event_simpleName=/FileWritten/ AND event_simpleName=/FileDeleted/

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

2026-07-27 16 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged fresh malicious cyber activity by a threat actor with ties to East Asia targeting government entities in the Middle East. ISO-delivered signed RegSchdTask.exe executed from non-standard/removable path AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the campaign's initial access: the legitimate ASUS-signed RegSchdTask.exe run from an ISO mount, user Temp, Downloads or Public dir rather than its real ASUS install directory. Article-specific because this binary is the sideload host used to load the TELESHIM DLL. Rationale: Anchored on the named ASUS sideload host RegSchdTask.exe (arrives via ISO) with a path exclusion — a signed scheduler utility running from Temp/ISO is the article's exact initial-access shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-hide-c2-traffic-inside-telegram/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ASUS software portable/troubleshooting run from a technician USB
  • Software packaging/repackaging labs staging ASUS utilities in Temp
  • IT deploying ASUS drivers from a network share extracted to a user path
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned sandbox
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe","asussetup.exe","asusdownloadlicense.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 against the article's hash list and check the parent — a mounted ISO (explorer.exe / DVD drive letter) or archive tool as parent is high-signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the RegSchdTask.exe/AsTaskSched.dll pair from the same folder. 3) Hunt: on the same device pivot to DeviceImageLoadEvents for AsTaskSched.dll and DeviceNetworkEvents to api.telegram.org within the next hour.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "RegSchdTask.exe"
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\", @"\Windows\"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\RegSchdTask.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has @"\Program Files" and NewProcessName !has @"\Windows\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TELESHIM DLL side-load: RegSchdTask.exe loads rogue AsTaskSched.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the TELESHIM sideload event itself — the ASUS RegSchdTask.exe process loading a non-Microsoft AsTaskSched.dll from a non-standard path. This is the moment the 32-bit TELESHIM backdoor gets execution inside a trusted process. Rationale: Uses the exact parent/module pair named by Zscaler (RegSchdTask.exe -> AsTaskSched.dll); an ASUS scheduler loading a DLL of that name is unique to this intrusion. Falcon FDR does not ship a module-load event type, hence empty falcon query. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-telegram-bots-secret-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1497
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • QA/reverse-engineering lab replaying the sample
  • Backup/restore repopulating an old ASUS install folder
  • EDR sensor re-baselining image loads after agent upgrade
Suppression filter
| where not(SHA256 in~ ("")) or FolderPath !has @"\ASUS\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash AsTaskSched.dll and confirm it is unsigned / not signed by ASUSTeK vs the article hashes. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the DLL, and kill the RegSchdTask.exe process tree. 3) Hunt: check the same host/hour for outbound HTTPS to api.telegram.org and for a second sideload pair GoProAlertService.exe + pthreadVC2.dll.

| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Program Files\"))

| order by Timestamp desc

| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| where EventData has "AsTaskSched.dll" and EventData has "RegSchdTask.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventData

Telegram Bot API used for C2 by non-browser/non-messaging process AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the core TELESHIM C2 channel: a process that is not a browser or the Telegram desktop client initiating connections to api.telegram.org / core.telegram.org. Article-specific because TELESHIM stores an encrypted bot token + chat ID and beacons to the Telegram Bot API to blend with legitimate traffic. Rationale: Pivots on api.telegram.org/core.telegram.org (confirmed by Zscaler as the TELESHIM C2 host) plus a browser/Telegram-client exclusion so only unexpected processes surface. Sentinel path uses DNS (ImDnsActivity) because process-attributed egress is not natively available in that schema. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-hide-c2-traffic-inside-telegram/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom PowerShell/Python scripts using Telegram bots for internal alerting
  • Monitoring/CI agents posting build status to a Telegram channel
  • curl/wget one-off tests against the Telegram API by a developer
  • Third-party notification middleware bundled in an EXE contacting Telegram
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("python.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell.exe","node.exe","curl.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and its signer/hash; a signed ASUS/GoPro utility or an unsigned binary from Temp beaconing to Telegram is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block api.telegram.org egress for that asset group, and capture the process memory for the encrypted bot token/chat ID. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts talking to the Telegram API from the same process name and pivot to BINDCLOAK domains cert.hypersnet.com / ssl.blsouqs.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.telegram.org","core.telegram.org")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("telegram.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","teams.exe","ms-teams.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Queries=make_set(DnsQuery) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc

TELESHIM/MIXEDKEY sideload host binary beacons to Telegram (C2 + exfil) AIActions on Objectives High
High-fidelity variant scoped to the two named sideload hosts (RegSchdTask.exe, GoProAlertService.exe) sending traffic to the Telegram Bot API. TELESHIM registers the host by MAC and chunk-exfiltrates command output over this channel, so these binaries reaching Telegram is the campaign's C2/exfil signature. Rationale: Two named-binary anchors (RegSchdTask.exe / GoProAlertService.exe) plus the telegram.org destination make this near-zero-FP — neither an ASUS scheduler nor a GoPro alert service has any legitimate reason to reach the Telegram API. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://cyberpress.org/teleshim-targets-middle-east-governments/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated legitimate GoPro desktop service phoning home (not to Telegram — excluded by destination)
  • Endpoint proxy rewriting SNI causing mislabeled RemoteUrl
  • Threat-intel detonation of the sample in a monitored VM
  • Renamed internal utility coincidentally named RegSchdTask.exe on a build box
Response runbook
1) Triage: this pairing is malicious by design — validate the host is impacted, not a sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate immediately, block telegram.org egress for the asset, and preserve process memory to recover the bot token/chat ID for C2 takedown. 3) Hunt: search proxy/DNS org-wide for the same process->telegram.org pattern and correlate with reconnaissance commands (whoami, ipconfig, net) executed 4:00-12:00 UTC.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("RegSchdTask.exe","GoProAlertService.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "telegram.org" or RemoteUrl has_any ("api.telegram.org","core.telegram.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("RegSchdTask.exe","GoProAlertService.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "telegram.org"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MIXEDKEY encrypted payload: .PCPKEY file dropped on disk AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the environmentally-keyed final payload MIXEDKEY reflectively loads — files with the unusual .PCPKEY extension (e.g. C99F29AC08454855B3D538960BB2F34F.PCPKEY). The extension is unique to this campaign and encrypted with a key derived from the volume serial number. Rationale: The .PCPKEY extension (with the concrete sample C99F29AC08454855B3D538960BB2F34F.PCPKEY) is a bespoke campaign artifact with no legitimate software use, making a bare extension match high-fidelity and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-telegram-bots-secret-backdoor/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated proprietary app coincidentally using a .PCPKEY extension (rare)
  • Backup software copying a previously dropped payload during restore
  • Forensic tooling writing a captured sample back to disk during analysis
  • EDR quarantine restore recreating the file
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess writing the .PCPKEY file — GoProAlertService.exe or pthreadVC2.dll context confirms MIXEDKEY. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the .PCPKEY file plus the GoProAlertService.exe/pthreadVC2.dll pair. 3) Hunt: pivot to the parent sideload (RegSchdTask.exe/TELESHIM) and outbound BINDCLOAK C2 to cert.hypersnet.com; collect the volume serial number for payload decryption.

| where FileName endswith ".PCPKEY"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

BINDCLOAK C2 beacon to cert.hypersnet.com / ssl.blsouqs.com AICommand & Control High
Detects the final-stage BINDCLOAK implant contacting its C2 infrastructure. Article-specific IOC-driven detection on the confirmed BINDCLOAK domain cert.hypersnet.com plus the campaign domain ssl.blsouqs.com, covering both resolution (DNS) and connection telemetry. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the two second-source-confirmed campaign domains (cert.hypersnet.com is BINDCLOAK's named C2). Sentinel path corrected to DnsEvents.Name (IPAddresses is not a DnsEvents column). Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-hide-c2-traffic-inside-telegram/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Passive DNS/threat-intel scanner resolving the IOC domain from a research host
  • Security appliance sinkhole logging the domain
  • Analyst manually browsing the IOC for validation
  • DNS logging duplicate from a forwarder replaying old queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and host; any internal asset resolving cert.hypersnet.com/ssl.blsouqs.com outside a sanctioned research VM is a confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: isolate the host, sinkhole/block both domains at DNS and proxy, and snapshot memory for the 64-bit BINDCLOAK implant. 3) Hunt: trace back the TELESHIM->MIXEDKEY->BINDCLOAK chain on the host and sweep for other assets resolving the same domains or matching the sample hashes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("cert.hypersnet.com","ssl.blsouqs.com")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("cert.hypersnet.com","ssl.blsouqs.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryTypeName, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TELESHIM/MIXEDKEY/BINDCLOAK known-bad file hash execution AIInstallation Medium
IOC hash sweep for the campaign's PE samples across process creation, module loads and file writes. Surfaces any host that executed or wrote a TELESHIM, MIXEDKEY or BINDCLOAK sample by SHA256/MD5. Rationale: Hash-based sweep using the 8 SHA256 + 5 MD5 samples from the article's IOC bundle; exact-hash matches are definitionally low-FP and cover process, module-load and file-write surfaces. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in a monitored lab
  • EDR retro-scan re-hashing a quarantined file
  • Threat-intel platform ingesting the sample into a detonation sandbox on the corporate network
  • Backup indexing a previously captured artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the match is a live host not a sandbox, and note which stage (TELESHIM/MIXEDKEY/BINDCLOAK) the hash maps to. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine all matching files, and block the associated Telegram and hypersnet/blsouqs C2. 3) Hunt: expand to the full kill chain on the host (sideload pairs, .PCPKEY drop, C2 beacons) and sweep the fleet for the same hashes and reconnaissance activity in the 4:00-12:00 UTC operator window.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub Adds 3-Day Dependabot Cooldown to Limit Poisoned Package Adoption

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 5 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

GitHub has announced a new cooldown mechanism in Dependabot, allowing the tool to wait at least three days after a release is published before opening a pull request. "The cooldown configuration option in the dependabot.yml still controls the behavior, though, so you can choose a different cooldown parameter that fits your project," the Microsoft-owned subsidiary said. Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

CISA KEV
2026-07-27 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet FortiOS contains an exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor vulnerability. This may allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to bypass the patch developed for the symbolic link persistency mechanism observed in some post-exploit cases, via crafted HTTP requests. An attacker would need first to have compromised the product via another vulnerability, at filesystem level. Vendor: Fortinet, Product: FortiOS. Federal patch due: 2026-08-10.

Phishing email from npm-lookalike domain npmjs.help AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail sent from, or containing links to, the npmjs.help lookalike domain used to phish npm maintainers ('qix'/chalk-debug campaign) into surrendering 2FA/credentials on a fake npm support portal. Article-specific: npmjs.help is a typosquat of the legitimate npmjs.com and has no benign use. Rationale: Uses the exact IOC npmjs.help; a corroborated typosquat of npmjs.com used to send support@npmjs.help phishing to npm maintainers — any inbound mail from it or containing its URLs is malicious with near-zero legitimate traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/20-popular-npm-packages-compromised-chalk-debug-strip-ansi-color-convert-wrap-ansi • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/chalk-and-17-other-npm-packages-compromised-in-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness team forwarding a captured phishing sample internally for training
  • Threat-intel analyst emailing the IOC domain string in the body of a report (matched by the Recipients/body has-clause)
  • A quarantined message surfacing in a defender/SOC review mailbox rather than a real inbox delivery
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation !in ("Quarantine","Blocked") or isempty(DeliveryLocation)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation for each hit — anything Delivered/Inbox to a live user is priority; identify recipients who are package maintainers or have npm/PyPI publishing rights. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message org-wide (Explorer or Search-and-Purge), block npmjs.help at the mail gateway and web proxy, and force credential + npm/PyPI token reset for any recipient who interacted. 3) Hunt: check UrlClickEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents for anyone who reached npmjs.help (see companion UC), and review recent package publishes / token creations from those maintainer accounts.

| order by TimeGenerated desc
Endpoint DNS/HTTP connection to npm-phish portal npmjs.help AIExploitation High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to npmjs.help — the fake npm support/2FA portal from the chalk-debug maintainer-phishing campaign. A hit means a user reached the credential-harvesting site, the step immediately preceding npm account takeover and malicious package publication. Rationale: Matches the exact corroborated IOC npmjs.help at the DNS/HTTP layer; the domain is a typosquat with no legitimate destination, so any endpoint reaching it is a maintainer interacting with the credential-harvest portal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/20-popular-npm-packages-compromised-chalk-debug-strip-ansi-color-convert-wrap-ansi
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst manually browsing to npmjs.help during IOC verification/sandboxing
  • Secure web gateway or URL-detonation sandbox pre-fetching the link from a quarantined email
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion tool performing passive DNS enrichment on the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user, and InitiatingProcess — a real browser (chrome/msedge/firefox) reaching npmjs.help from a maintainer workstation is high severity; a proxy/sandbox appliance is likely benign. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block npmjs.help at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a browser hit is confirmed, and immediately rotate the user's npm/PyPI credentials, session tokens, and publish/automation tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate with the companion email UC for the delivering message, and review that maintainer's npm/PyPI account for new tokens, 2FA changes, or package versions published in the following days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let win = 30d;
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(win) | where Name has "npmjs.help" | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, Client=ClientIP, Query=Name, QueryType),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(win) | where DnsQuery has "npmjs.help" | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, Client=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryType),
(ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(win) | where Url has "npmjs.help" | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, Client=SrcIpAddr, Query=Url)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Steam discussion forums are being abused in ClickFix attacks that pretend to be fixes for game and computer problems but actually infect devices with cryptominers. [...]

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Steam forum ClickFix attacks infect gamers with XMRig cryptominers
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Microsoft Defender path exclusion added for C:\Windows\Background (ClickFix XMRig) · [LLM] Scheduled task 'XMRig-<host>' launching C:\Windows\Background\system.exe as SYSTEM · [LLM] Payload written to C:\Windows\Background\system.exe (XMRig drop) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection / DNS to msfconfig.icu (XMRig payload download) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XMRig miner executing as SYSTEM from C:\Windows\Background
Microsoft Defender path exclusion added for C:\Windows\Background (ClickFix XMRig) AIInstallation High
Hunts the ClickFix/msf-utility campaign registering C:\Windows\Background as a Defender scan exclusion before dropping system.exe. Legitimate software almost never excludes a folder directly under C:\Windows, making the exclusion path itself high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the exact defense-evasion artifact from the article — a Defender exclusion for C:\Windows\Background — which is a fixed, campaign-specific path. Corroborated by TechEchelon and daily.dev write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise EDR/AV migration scripts that add temporary exclusions during agent installs
  • Backup or imaging software that legitimately excludes a staging folder (rarely under C:\Windows though)
  • Sysadmin manually running Add-MpPreference during troubleshooting (would not target C:\Windows\Background)
  • In-house build/CI tooling excluding artifact directories
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and RegistryValueData !has @"C:\Windows\Background")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): On the alerting host, run Get-MpPreference to confirm C:\Windows\Background is an active exclusion and check whether the folder and system.exe exist. Identify the initiating account/process. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate the host, remove the exclusion (Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath 'C:\Windows\Background'), then delete the XMRig scheduled task and the folder. Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on the same host and org for outbound traffic to msfconfig.icu, a scheduled task named XMRig-*, and other hosts with the same exclusion path.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValueName has "Background" or RegistryValueData has @"C:\Windows\Background"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValue has "Background" or RegistryValueData has @"C:\Windows\Background"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(Add|Set)-MpPreference/i CommandLine=/ExclusionPath/i | regex("Background", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

Scheduled task 'XMRig-<host>' launching C:\Windows\Background\system.exe as SYSTEM AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the campaign's persistence mechanism: a scheduled task prefixed 'XMRig-' that runs system.exe from C:\Windows\Background with SYSTEM privileges at every boot. The task name prefix and target path are both hardcoded and campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the two hardcoded campaign strings — task-name prefix 'XMRig-' and target binary C:\Windows\Background\system.exe — so it fires only on this specific persistence, not generic schtasks usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin task named with 'XMRig' during malware-removal/testing
  • Security researcher reproducing the sample in a lab
  • EDR remediation script that recreates then deletes the task to clean it
  • None expected in normal enterprise operation — the path C:\Windows\Background is non-standard
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SenseIR.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "/delete")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Run schtasks /query /tn XMRig-<hostname> /v and confirm the action points to C:\Windows\Background\system.exe and runs as SYSTEM. Note the creating account and time. Step 2 (Contain): Delete the task (schtasks /delete /tn XMRig-<hostname> /f), kill running system.exe/xmrig processes, isolate host. Step 3 (Hunt): Check the same host for the Defender exclusion and msfconfig.icu connections; sweep the fleet for any XMRig-* task or system.exe under C:\Windows\Background.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "XMRig-" or ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\Windows\Background\system.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe" or CommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask"
| where CommandLine has "XMRig-" or CommandLine has @"\Windows\Background\system.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection / DNS to msfconfig.icu (XMRig payload download) AICommand & Control High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the campaign C2 msfconfig.icu, from which the XMRig payload is pulled over TCP/443 at /tmp/system.txt. The domain is a dedicated attacker-controlled indicator with no legitimate use. Rationale: msfconfig.icu is a dedicated attacker domain confirmed by multiple write-ups; any resolution or connection to it (or a fetch of /tmp/system.txt) is a direct hit with essentially no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers • https://daily.dev/posts/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers-keosw3y2g
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst or sandbox detonating the sample and resolving the domain
  • Security tool actively probing/sinkholing the IOC
  • DNS security appliance logging a blocked-but-attempted lookup (still worth reviewing)
  • No benign business use of a .icu 'msfconfig' domain is expected
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify which process on the host initiated the lookup/connection (expect powershell.exe) and whether a file was written to C:\Windows\Background afterward. Step 2 (Contain): Block msfconfig.icu at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and remove the temporary firewall allow-rule the script created. Step 3 (Hunt): Sweep DNS/proxy logs org-wide for msfconfig.icu, and on any matching host look for system.exe, the XMRig-* task, and the Defender exclusion.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "msfconfig.icu" or RemoteUrl endswith "/tmp/system.txt"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery =~ "msfconfig.icu" or DnsQuery endswith ".msfconfig.icu"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Payload written to C:\Windows\Background\system.exe (XMRig drop) AIInstallation High
Hunts the file-write of the downloaded XMRig payload to the campaign's fixed install directory C:\Windows\Background. This directory is created by the malware and is not a legitimate Windows path, so any executable written there is suspicious. Rationale: C:\Windows\Background is a fixed, malware-created directory named explicitly in the article; any file write there (system.exe or config.json) is a durable install-stage indicator distinct from the network and persistence pivots. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A third-party app that coincidentally creates a 'Background' subfolder under a different root (query is anchored to C:\Windows\Background specifically)
  • Analyst restoring/extracting the sample into the same path during investigation
  • Backup software re-writing the folder during recovery testing
  • No legitimate Windows component writes to C:\Windows\Background
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Hash system.exe and submit to your sandbox/VT; confirm it is XMRig and capture FileOriginUrl (expect msfconfig.icu). Identify the writing process. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate host, stop/kill xmrig and system processes, delete C:\Windows\Background and its contents after preserving a sample. Step 3 (Hunt): Correlate with the XMRig-* scheduled task, the Defender exclusion, and msfconfig.icu traffic on this and other hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\Background"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileOriginUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\Windows\Background"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XMRig miner executing as SYSTEM from C:\Windows\Background AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of the miner itself — a process running from C:\Windows\Background (system.exe, or a process masquerading as 'system'/'xmrig') typically launched by the scheduler at SYSTEM integrity. This catches the resource-hijacking stage even if the drop/persistence events were missed. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact execution artifact — a binary named system.exe/xmrig.exe running out of C:\Windows\Background — a masqueraded location + name that no legitimate Windows process uses, catching the impact stage independently of the drop. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers
ATT&CKT1496 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst executing the recovered sample in an isolated lab
  • EDR detonation chamber replaying the binary
  • Legitimate 'System' process is C:\Windows\System32-based and will not match the C:\Windows\Background path filter
  • No benign software ships a system.exe/xmrig.exe under C:\Windows\Background
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Confirm the parent is a scheduler/svchost (SYSTEM launch) and check CPU utilisation; hash the image to confirm XMRig. Step 2 (Contain): Kill the process tree, disable/delete the XMRig-* task, isolate the host, and remove C:\Windows\Background plus the Defender exclusion. Step 3 (Hunt): Look for msfconfig.icu beaconing/pool traffic and enumerate other hosts running system.exe from C:\Windows\Background or holding the XMRig-* task.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\Background"
| where FileName in~ ("system.exe","xmrig.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\Background"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\system.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\xmrig.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TokenElevationType, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
