Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1059.001

Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 16 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

SourTrade malvertising infrastructure contact (campaign domains + Bun-runtime host) AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS resolution / network connections to the published SourTrade landing-page and secondary-runtime domains, including purelogicbox.org which serves the clean Bun runtime. This is the delivery-infrastructure IOC pivot for the browser-assembled malware campaign detailed by Confiant. Rationale: Uses the concrete SourTrade domain IOCs published by Confiant and re-counted by The Hacker News (purelogicbox.org is specifically the Bun-runtime host). Domain-list resolution from a browser is high-fidelity because these are single-purpose malvertising domains with no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-sites-use-javascript-to-build-malware-in-browser-memory/
ATT&CKT1189 T1583.008
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating a SourTrade sample intentionally
  • Threat-intel platform or URL-scanning appliance crawling the IOC domains
  • A future benign re-registration of an expired campaign domain (domains rotate)
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS logging the block as a query event
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MonitoringHost.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("sandbox-detonation-host")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved the domain and the initiating browser process; check whether a same-session .exe download landed in Downloads (pivot to UC2). 2) Contain: block the domain(s) at the DNS/proxy layer, isolate the host if an executable was written, and reset any trading/wallet credentials the user may have entered on the fake landing page. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the full 96-domain SourTrade set, look for browser-written .exe files with FileOriginUrl on any campaign domain, and review ad-referral chains that led the user to the landing page.

Browser-assembled SourTrade executable dropped with campaign-domain origin (MotW) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a browser process writing a .exe to disk whose Mark-of-the-Web download source (FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl) is a SourTrade landing-page domain, plus the three published sample hashes. This is the article-specific moment the in-browser-assembled Bun executable lands on disk — the point where per-session hash rotation is defeated by pivoting on origin rather than hash. Rationale: The Defender query pivots on FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl — the MotW record Confiant notes points at the landing page domain, not the Bun-runtime host — which survives the per-session hash rotation the campaign relies on. The three published SHA-256 samples are added as a direct fallback; Splunk/Falcon fall back to browser-written .exe in Downloads because CIM/FDR lack an origin-URL field. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://gbhackers.com/sourtrade-browser-assembled/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html
ATT&CKT1027 T1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers downloaded via browser to Downloads (very common on the hash-less fallback branch)
  • Portable apps or dev tools (e.g. genuine Bun/Node installers) saved by developers
  • Browser auto-update stub executables written to profile folders
  • Corporate software-portal downloads delivering signed .exe installers
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") and isempty(FileOriginUrl) and isempty(FileOriginReferrerUrl) and SHA256 !in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b","05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6","ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl resolves to a SourTrade domain (high-confidence branch) or that the .exe is unsigned/low-prevalence on the Downloads fallback branch; check the process tree for subsequent execution. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the origin domain, and isolate the host if the executable ran; because JSCEAL/WeevilProxy is the likely payload, treat as credential-theft — force-reset the user's trading, wallet, and SSO credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot the origin domain into UC1/UC3, look for a same-origin ServiceWorker /config fetch preceding the write, and scan for Bun-runtime standalone executables launched from Downloads across the fleet.

| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
| where (FileOriginUrl has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","campainter.digital","riovera.info","lunavo.club","hanzoa.digital","authcom.digital","fererro.digital","zythera.info","angelxc.digital","toushere.digital","auronix.digital","quorivamesh.digital","junora.digital","savanhe.digital","tenderi.digital"))
   or (FileOriginReferrerUrl has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","campainter.digital","riovera.info","lunavo.club","hanzoa.digital","authcom.digital","fererro.digital","zythera.info","angelxc.digital","toushere.digital","auronix.digital","quorivamesh.digital","junora.digital","savanhe.digital","tenderi.digital"))

SourTrade ServiceWorker build-instruction fetch (/config + /sw.js on campaign domains) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts web-proxy requests to the /sw.js ServiceWorker and /config build-instruction endpoints on SourTrade campaign domains — the exact same-origin paths the landing page uses to register the worker and pull the PE header, section table, .bun bytecode and secondary runtime URL. Scoped to the campaign domains, this catches the technique even as individual sample hashes rotate and helps surface newly-registered domains reusing the pattern. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim /sw.js and /config paths (article code blocks) scoped to the confirmed campaign domains — the ServiceWorker + build-instruction pattern is the campaign's signature and survives hash rotation. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because FDR and the available Datadog sources do not carry URL request paths and there is no AWS telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/sourtrade-malvertising-malware/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1189
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A future benign re-registration of an expired SourTrade domain serving a legitimate /config or /sw.js
  • Proxy logging a blocked request as an allowed event after policy change
  • Security scanner / crawler fetching the campaign paths during investigation
  • Rare legitimate PWA on a re-purposed domain registering a service worker at /sw.js
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host+user made the /config fetch and whether a /sw.js registration and secondary purelogicbox.org runtime fetch occurred in the same session; check for a subsequent browser-written .exe (UC2). 2) Contain: block the domain at the proxy, clear the browser's registered ServiceWorkers on the affected host, and isolate if an executable landed. 3) Hunt: expand to the full 96-domain list, generalize the hunt to any domain where a single client fetched /sw.js then /config then received a same-origin attachment download, and correlate the originating malicious ad-referral.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","campainter.digital","riovera.info","lunavo.club","hanzoa.digital","authcom.digital","fererro.digital","zythera.info","angelxc.digital","toushere.digital","auronix.digital","quorivamesh.digital","junora.digital","savanhe.digital","tenderi.digital")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/config","/sw.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where HttpHostName has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","campainter.digital","riovera.info","lunavo.club","hanzoa.digital","authcom.digital","fererro.digital","zythera.info","angelxc.digital","toushere.digital","auronix.digital","quorivamesh.digital","junora.digital","savanhe.digital","tenderi.digital")
| where Url has_any ("/config","/sw.js")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, FileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental

references:

logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows

    filter_known_good:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SourTrade browser-assembled .exe downloaded from campaign landing domains AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a browser writing an executable to disk whose mark-of-the-web origin URL is one of the confirmed SourTrade malvertising landing domains (fake TradingView/Solana/Luno). Because the malware is assembled in-memory and delivered via a same-origin ServiceWorker download, the dropped .exe carries the landing domain as its FileOriginUrl — the single cleanest host-side artifact of this technique. Rationale: Uses the 11 Confiant-confirmed SourTrade landing/staging domains as FileOriginUrl/FileOriginReferrerUrl on a browser-written .exe — the exact host-side residue of the same-origin ServiceWorker download. Splunk falls back to the 3 confirmed SHA256s since CIM Endpoint.Filesystem carries no origin-URL field. Cross-checked Confiant blog + The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html • https://gbhackers.com/sourtrade-browser-assembled/
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or threat-intel team intentionally detonating a SourTrade sample on a lab endpoint that ships MDE telemetry
  • Automated sandbox/detonation VM fetching the landing page for classification
  • A takedown/sinkhole researcher who now controls one of the listed domains serving a benign page
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platform re-hosting a lookalike lure on one of these domains
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the DeviceName/user, confirm the .exe FolderPath (Downloads/Temp), grab its SHA256 and check whether the process has already executed (DeviceProcessEvents on that hash/path). 2) Contain: isolate the host in MDE, quarantine/delete the dropped .exe, and block the source domain + its resolved IPs at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the other 10 domains (see C2 UC), for any Bun-runtime executable running under a non-bun name (see execution UC), and for credential-theft follow-on (browser cookie-store access, wallet-file reads).

SourTrade payload: Bun standalone runtime executing under a masqueraded name AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a Bun (Oven) standalone runtime executable running under a filename other than bun.exe from a user-writable path, or matching a confirmed SourTrade hash. SourTrade weaponises a clean Bun 'standalone' runtime as the payload container, so the compiled PE retains Bun/Oven version-info resources while being renamed to a fake trading/crypto app — a high-fidelity masquerade signal. Rationale: Confiant confirms the payload is built from a 'clean Bun standalone runtime', so the compiled PE inherits Bun/Oven version-info resources (OriginalFileName bun.exe, Product Bun, Company Oven) while being renamed — a durable masquerade heuristic that survives the per-session hash rotation. Known-sample hashes are OR-ed in for high-confidence hits; Falcon uses hashes only because FDR ProcessRollup2 lacks PE version-info fields. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/sourtrade-malvertising-malware/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running the output of 'bun build --compile' from their Downloads or project folder without customising PE metadata
  • A legitimate commercial app that bundles a Bun standalone runtime under its own product name
  • Bun itself copied/renamed by a build script into a Temp/AppData staging directory
  • CI/CD artifact of an internal Bun-compiled tool executed on a workstation
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "node_modules" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun.exe","node.exe","Code.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") or FolderPath has "\\.bun\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the on-disk name vs the Bun/Oven version info and the launch parent — a browser/explorer-launched Bun binary in Downloads named after a crypto/trading app is the true positive; a dev shell parent in a repo path is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the process image, capture the SHA256 and submit for analysis. 3) Hunt: on confirmation look for the stealer behaviours Bitdefender documented — local proxy setup, browser cookie/credential store access, keylogging hooks, screenshot capture, and crypto-wallet file reads, plus beacons to the SourTrade domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "bun.exe"
      or ProcessVersionInfoInternalFileName =~ "bun.exe"
      or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Bun"
      or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Oven")
| where FileName !~ "bun.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any ("Downloads","Temp","AppData")
   or SHA256 in ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b","05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6","ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where (ActingProcessFileOriginalName =~ "bun.exe"
      or ActingProcessFileInternalName =~ "bun.exe"
      or ActingProcessFileProduct has "Bun"
      or ActingProcessFileCompany has "Oven")
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "bun.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("Downloads","Temp","AppData")
   or SHA256 in ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b","05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6","ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, SHA256, ActingProcessFileProduct, ActingProcessFileOriginalName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SourTrade C2 / Bun-runtime staging domain resolution or connection AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/network activity to the confirmed SourTrade infrastructure — purelogicbox.org (the standaloneUrl serving the clean Bun runtime) and the landing/C2 domains. Catches both the in-browser fetch of the Bun runtime blob and post-infection payload callbacks (proxy/cookie/wallet exfil). Non-browser initiating processes reaching these domains are the highest-fidelity subset. Rationale: All 11 domains are Confiant-confirmed SourTrade infrastructure, with purelogicbox.org explicitly the standaloneUrl host for the clean Bun runtime blob. Surfacing the initiating process (NonBrowserInitiator flag) separates the benign in-browser fetch from post-exec payload C2 without dropping either. DNS-based expression ports cleanly across all five platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html • https://gbhackers.com/sourtrade-browser-assembled/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or takedown researcher deliberately resolving/browsing the IOC domains for validation
  • Security proxy or DNS-firewall that pre-resolves blocklist entries to build enforcement records
  • A sinkholed domain now pointing at a benign researcher-controlled host
  • Passive-DNS or scanning appliance in the environment enumerating the domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe","MpCmdRun.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a browser hitting the domain suggests a user landed on the malvertising page; a non-browser process (renamed Bun binary, script host) indicates active infection/C2. 2) Contain: sink the domains and resolved IPs at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate any host with a non-browser initiator. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host in DeviceFileEvents for a browser-dropped .exe (delivery UC) and DeviceProcessEvents for a masqueraded Bun runtime (execution UC); review browser credential/cookie store access and wallet-file reads for exfil scope.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","lunavo.club","authcom.digital","form-engine.digital","trustconnect.digital","predictcore.digital")
| extend NonBrowserInitiator = InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","chromium.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, NonBrowserInitiator, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by NonBrowserInitiator desc, Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","lunavo.club","authcom.digital","form-engine.digital","trustconnect.digital","predictcore.digital")

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShinyHunters data leaks fuel $2,000 sextortion email scam

BleepingComputer
2026-07-25 5 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors are using email addresses exposed in data breaches leaked by the ShinyHunters extortion group to send sextortion emails demanding $2,000 in Bitcoin. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1486

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Fake ShinyHunters sextortion email by fixed subject + spoofed display name · [LLM] ShinyHunters sextortion campaign fan-out (one subject, many random senders/recipients)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Fake ShinyHunters sextortion email by fixed subject + spoofed display name AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound emails carrying the exact ShinyHunters sextortion signature: subject 'Information about your online security' and/or display name 'ShinyHunters'/'You've Been HACKED'. Article-specific because it anchors on the campaign's fixed subject line and impersonated display names rather than generic extortion keywords. Rationale: Anchored on the campaign's two hardest signatures from the article: the verbatim subject 'Information about your online security' and the impersonated display names 'ShinyHunters'/'You've Been HACKED'. Both are unusual enough to be near-zero-FP; corroborated by second-source write-ups (MalwareTips, MyAntiSpyware, factually.co). Cross-checked against: • https://malwaretips.com/blogs/shinyhunters-hacking-group-email-scam-what-this-fake-sextortion-message-really-means/ • https://www.myantispyware.com/2026/07/06/fake-or-real-we-are-the-shinyhunters-hacking-group-email-scam-explained/
ATT&CKT1656 T1566 T1657
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security-awareness team forwarding a sample of the scam email to users as a warning (subject preserved)
  • SOC/phishing-mailbox auto-forward of a reported copy re-ingested as inbound
  • A legitimate vendor security newsletter that happens to use the phrase 'information about your online security' in a subject
  • Threat-intel or DFIR analyst mailing a captured specimen to a shared analysis mailbox
Suppression filter
| where RecipientEmailAddress !in~ ("phishing@yourorg.com","soc@yourorg.com","abuse@yourorg.com") and SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourorg.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the message is the sextortion template — check SenderFromAddress is a random/free-mail address inconsistent with the impersonated 'ShinyHunters' display name, and that SenderIPv4/SPF/DKIM fail. Verify no attachment or credential-harvest URL. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine via a purge across all matched RecipientEmailAddress values (same subject cluster), block the sender address/domain, and notify targeted users not to pay or reply. 3) Hunt: pivot on the subject to find the full recipient set (UC2 fan-out), and cross-reference recipients against known ShinyHunters-breach exposure (Amtrak, CarGurus, Betterment, ADT, Panera, Substack, Hallmark, McGraw Hill) to gauge which client lists were scraped.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject =~ "Information about your online security"
    or SenderDisplayName has_any ("ShinyHunters", "You've Been HACKED")
| where DeliveryAction != "Blocked"    // surface what actually landed in the mailbox
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderIPv4, SenderFromDomain, Subject, RecipientEmailAddress, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Subject =~ "Information about your online security"
    or Sender has_any ("ShinyHunters", "You've Been HACKED")
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, Sender, P2Sender, Recipients, Subject, MessageId, ClientIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.direction=inbound (All_Email.subject="Information about your online security" OR All_Email.src_user="ShinyHunters" OR All_Email.src_user="You've Been HACKED") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.src, All_Email.subject, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.message_id | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.direction=inbound (All_Email.subject="Information about your online security" OR All_Email.src_user="ShinyHunters" OR All_Email.src_user="You've Been HACKED") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.src, All_Email.subject, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.message_id | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
ShinyHunters sextortion campaign fan-out (one subject, many random senders/recipients) AIDelivery High
Detects the bulk nature of the campaign: a single fixed subject or impersonated display name delivered to many recipients from many disposable sender addresses within a window. This is a volume/fan-out pivot distinct from the single-message signature and catches variants that mutate the sender but reuse the lure. Rationale: Uses the same fixed subject/display-name anchors but pivots on fan-out — many disposable SenderFromAddress values blasting one lure to many recipients is the operational fingerprint the article describes (random sender addresses spoofing the ShinyHunters name). High-recipient + high-distinct-sender on a single subject is a strong campaign signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/shinyhunters-data-leaks-fuel-2-000-sextortion-email-scam/ • https://malwaretips.com/blogs/shinyhunters-hacking-group-email-scam-what-this-fake-sextortion-message-really-means/
ATT&CKT1566 T1656 T1657
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate bulk security-notification email (e.g. breach-notice mailing) that shares a similar subject and legitimately reaches many recipients from a small sender set — distinguishable by DistinctSenders being 1-2
  • Awareness team deliberately mailing the scam sample to a distribution list
  • Newsletter/marketing blast whose subject coincidentally matches — check SPF/DKIM pass and a single trusted sender domain
  • Load-testing or phishing-simulation platform sending templated messages to many staff
Suppression filter
| where DistinctSenders >= 2     // genuine campaigns spray from many disposable froms; legit bulk mail uses 1 trusted sender
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the aggregated row — high Recipients with high DistinctSenders (many disposable froms) confirms a blast; inspect SampleSenders/SampleSenderIPs for free-mail or bulletproof ranges and check auth (SPF/DKIM/DMARC failures). 2) Contain: bulk-quarantine/purge the whole subject cluster across all recipients, add the sender addresses/IPs to the block list, and push a broadcast advisory that the email is a scam and no payment/reply is warranted. 3) Hunt: enumerate every targeted RecipientEmailAddress and correlate against the ShinyHunters-leaked datasets named in the article (Amtrak, CarGurus, Betterment, ADT, Panera Bread, Substack, Hallmark, McGraw Hill) to identify which breach exposure fed the target list and flag those users for heightened phishing monitoring.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject =~ "Information about your online security"
    or SenderDisplayName has_any ("ShinyHunters", "You've Been HACKED")
| summarize Recipients = dcount(RecipientEmailAddress),
            DistinctSenders = dcount(SenderFromAddress),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleSenders = make_set(SenderFromAddress, 15),
            SampleSenderIPs = make_set(SenderIPv4, 15)
        by Subject
| where Recipients >= 5     // 5 = low bar for a coordinated blast vs a one-off; tune up in large tenants
| order by Recipients desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Subject =~ "Information about your online security"
    or Sender has_any ("ShinyHunters", "You've Been HACKED")
| summarize Recipients = dcount(tostring(Recipients)),
            DistinctSenders = dcount(Sender),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleSenders = make_set(Sender, 15),
            SampleClientIPs = make_set(ClientIP, 15)
        by Subject
| where Recipients >= 5
| order by Recipients desc
CLOUD

| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Email.recipient) as recipients dc(All_Email.src) as distinct_senders count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Email.src) as sender_addresses from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.direction=inbound (All_Email.subject="Information about your online security" OR All_Email.src_user="ShinyHunters" OR All_Email.src_user="You've Been HACKED") by All_Email.subject | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | where recipients>=5 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - recipients

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

Fastjson 1.x RCE Vulnerability Targeted in Attacks With No Patched Available

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 15 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Security firms ThreatBook and Imperva say attackers are targeting a critical flaw in Fastjson, Alibaba's JSON library for Java. In affected Spring Boot applications, a malicious JSON request can execute code without authentication, with the privileges of the Java process. Tracked as CVE-2026-16723, the vulnerability carries an Alibaba-assigned CVSS score of 9.0. The confirmed chain requires

CVEsCVE-2026-16723
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Fastjson 1.x CVE-2026-16723 exploit payload in inbound JSON (@type + nested JAR / /proc/self/fd) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Spring Boot Java process spawning shell/LOLBin child (Fastjson RCE execution) · [LLM] Web shell (.jsp/.jspx/.war) written by Java process post-Fastjson RCE · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Java (fat-JAR) outbound fetch of remote JAR / SSRF egress to public IP (CVE-2026
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Fastjson 1.x CVE-2026-16723 exploit payload in inbound JSON (@type + nested JAR / /proc/self/fd) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to Spring Boot apps carrying the Fastjson deserialization exploit signature: an attacker-controlled @type combined with a nested JAR path (!/), a /proc/self/fd reference, or an @JSONType trust-signal annotation. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact type-resolution abuse strings Firsov described for CVE-2026-16723, not generic JSON traffic. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE-2026-16723 type-confusion strings from Firsov's analysis (@type turned into class-resource lookup, nested JAR path, /proc/self/fd newer-JDK path, @JSONType trust signal) rather than generic JSON. Both ThreatBook and Imperva confirmed in-the-wild request activity, so the payload shape is corroborated across two vendors per the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Fastjson clients that intentionally send @type for polymorphic deserialization between trusted internal services
  • Security scanners / pentest tooling (Nessus, Burp) probing the endpoint with the same signature
  • API payloads that reference a .jar download URL for benign artifact-management workflows
  • WAF logging its own normalized/decoded copy of a request, double-counting a single event
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<internal-scanner-ip-not-applicable>") | where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Burp"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body for the matched event and confirm the @type value resolves to an attacker class plus a nested JAR/proc-fd reference; identify the target host and Fastjson version via dependency inventory. 2) Contain: if the app runs Fastjson 1.2.68–1.2.83 with SafeMode disabled, block the source IP at the WAF and apply -Dfastjson.parser.safeMode=true or swap to fastjson:1.2.83_noneautotype, then restart the JVM. 3) Hunt: pivot to the app host for java.exe child processes, outbound JAR fetches, and new .jsp/.war files created after the request timestamp.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (RequestURL has "@type" or Message has "@type" or RequestContext has "@type")
| where (RequestURL has_any ("/proc/self/fd",".jar!/","!/","@JSONType") or Message has_any ("/proc/self/fd",".jar!/","!/","@JSONType") or RequestContext has_any ("/proc/self/fd",".jar!/","!/","@JSONType"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Spring Boot Java process spawning shell/LOLBin child (Fastjson RCE execution) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a java/javaw process (the Spring Boot fat-JAR) spawning a command interpreter or download LOLBin, the expected post-exploitation step once CVE-2026-16723 achieves code execution with the Java process privileges. Article-specific because the exploit runs in-process inside the fat-JAR loader, so java as the parent of cmd/sh/curl on a server is the tell. Rationale: CVE-2026-16723 executes in-process inside the Spring Boot fat-JAR loader, so java.exe as parent of a shell or download LOLBin on a web-tier host is the highest-fidelity execution pivot. Parent+child pairing (not bare java) keeps FP down per house style.
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD or build agents where Java (Maven/Gradle) legitimately shells out to git/curl/sh
  • App-server management scripts invoking whoami/net for health checks
  • Elasticsearch/Logstash or other Java daemons spawning helper binaries by design
  • Java-based monitoring agents running certutil/nslookup diagnostics
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\jenkins\\","\\buildagent\\","\\gradle\\","\\.m2\\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("maven","gradle","jenkins"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for reconnaissance (whoami, id), download (curl/wget/certutil), or reverse-shell strings, and confirm the java parent is the internet-facing Spring Boot app. 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the java process tree; block any download URL observed in the child command line. 3) Hunt: correlate with the WAF Fastjson-payload detection on the same host/time, then look for dropped web shells and outbound JAR fetches from the same java PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","nslookup.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","/java","\\java")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","/sh","/bash","bash","curl","wget","whoami","certutil.exe","nslookup.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget","whoami.exe","whoami","certutil.exe","nslookup.exe","bitsadmin.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

Java (fat-JAR) outbound fetch of remote JAR / SSRF egress to public IP (CVE-2026 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-16723 remote-JAR / SSRF stage: the Spring Boot java process (or an outbound web session) reaching a public IP to fetch attacker-controlled bytecode as a .jar or via a nested-JAR URL. Article-specific because ThreatBook's embedded-Tomcat test produced exactly this remote-JAR-fetch/SSRF behaviour for the vulnerability. Rationale: Anchors on ThreatBook's reproduced remote-JAR-fetch/SSRF outcome for CVE-2026-16723 and Firsov's /proc/self/fd remote-JAR path: an internet-facing Spring Boot java process initiating an outbound connection to a public IP for a .jar is anomalous. Sentinel clause matches the JAR/nested-JAR URL on ImNetworkSession (valid columns only).
ATT&CKT1105 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java apps auto-downloading dependencies/plugins from public Maven/Nexus repos at runtime
  • JVM auto-update or telemetry pings to vendor endpoints on 443
  • Legitimate SSRF-like integrations where the app fetches remote resources by design (webhooks, RSS)
  • NAT egress causing an internal repo to appear as a public IP in flow logs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("repo1.maven.org","repo.maven.apache.org","jcenter.bintray.com","nexus","artifactory"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the destination IP/URL reputation and confirm the fetched object is a .jar or nested-JAR path; verify the java process is the internet-facing Spring Boot app, not a build tool. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress/firewall and, if malicious, isolate the host and capture the downloaded artifact for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot to child processes of the same java PID and any newly written .jsp/.class/.jar files, and check the WAF for the preceding @type payload from the same source.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteUrl has_any (".jar","!/","/proc/self/fd") or RemotePort in (80, 8080, 8443)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort

Web shell (.jsp/.jspx/.war) written by Java process post-Fastjson RCE AIInstallation High
Hunts a java/javaw process writing a JSP/JSPX/WAR file, the classic web-shell drop that follows successful Fastjson CVE-2026-16723 code execution inside a Spring Boot app. Article-specific because the advisory explicitly tells defenders to inspect affected systems for web shells and unexpected file changes from the Java process. Rationale: The Alibaba/vendor guidance in the article explicitly names web shells and file changes as the post-exploitation IOC to inspect for. A java process creating a .jsp/.jspx/.war is very rare outside deployment automation, making this an alerting-grade, low-FP install-phase detection.
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate application deployment where the app server explodes a .war or generates JSPs to its work/ compile directory (Tomcat Jasper)
  • CI/CD auto-deploy writing new .war files into webapps/
  • Hot-reload / dev frameworks regenerating precompiled JSPs at runtime
  • Backup or migration tooling running under the Java service account restoring web content
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\work\\Catalina\\" and FolderPath !has "/work/Catalina/" and FolderPath !has "\\temp\\" and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("deploy","jenkins","catalina") and FolderPath has "webapps")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file and check for web-shell markers (Runtime.exec, request-parameter command execution, base64 eval) and confirm the folder is a web-served directory rather than a Jasper work/ compile path. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and reset any credentials reachable from the Java service context. 3) Hunt: correlate to the preceding Fastjson @type WAF payload and java child-process/network detections on the same host, and search other web servers for the same file hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".jspx" or FileName endswith ".war"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","/java","\\java")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".jsp" or TargetFileName endswith ".jspx" or TargetFileName endswith ".war"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
